terms.comment: The thief who steals by stealth; in comedy also a term of abuse, ‘you thief!’ (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Hor. S. 1.3.106: nē quis fūr esset, neu latrō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: One who robs by force, on the road or in a band; in Plautus still a hired soldier (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: nocturnus cum fūr pānem mīsisset canī, objectō temptāns an cibō posset capī
phrases.english: when a thief in the night threw a dog some bread, trying whether the food would win him over

phrases.latin: arca, quod arcēbantur fūrēs ab eā clausā
phrases.english: a chest (arca), because when it was shut thieves were kept off (arcēbantur) from it

arca.html: Varro’s etymology is right: de Vaan 50–51, s.v. arca, derives the noun from the root of arceō, ‘to contain, keep out’.
